definition: The unnatural register of translated text: source-language structures showing through, over-literal phrasing.
details: The unnatural register of translated text: source-language structures showing through, over-literal phrasing. Corpora built by machine-translating English into Arabic inherit it, and models trained on them speak translated Arabic rather than Arabic; native-authored data is the antidote.

explainer.lead: Translationese is the telltale unnatural register of translated text, where source-language structures and over-literal phrasing show through. It matters because models trained on machine-translated corpora learn to produce stilted output rather than natural language.

tiers.eli5: It's like a translated instruction manual that sounds slightly off, because the translator followed the original words too closely instead of writing the way people actually talk.
tiers.practitioner: When building a corpus by machine-translating English into Arabic, engineers risk training models that speak translated Arabic rather than Arabic. The fix is mixing in native-authored data.
tiers.paperLevel: Translationese is characterized by source-language structures surfacing in the target text and over-literal phrasing; it is observed in corpora built by machine translation and cannot be removed by the translation step alone.

explainer.example: A corpus machine-translated from English into Arabic teaches a model the register of translated Arabic, so it produces that register at inference; supplementing with native-authored Arabic corrects it.
